utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 19th of August, 2009. I would like, first and foremost, to welcome Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Petkovic, without forgetting Mr. Pusic, who is temporarily absent, as well as Mr. Coric. I would also like to include in my greetings Defence counsel, Mr. Karnavas more specifically, who's back, the OTP members and Mr. Stringer, who is going to resume his cross-examination, without forgetting all those people assisting us in these proceedings. That said, I shall now give the floor to Mr. Stringer so that he can resume his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone else in the courtroom. Mr. President, I'd like to introduce to the Trial Chamber an intern who has just joined our team for a few months. She's seated behind me. Tamara Blagojevic has completed her legal studies. She's working in the criminal court system in Belgrade, and she may be appearing in the courtroom in the coming months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber welcomes her and wishes her a good training with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, before we continue with the topics that we were discussing yesterday, I'd like to take a small detour to come back to something that relates to a different part of your testimony yesterday. At one point during your testimony yesterday, I think you'll recall, I put it to you that hundreds or thousands of Muslims were expelled from Mostar during the summer or spring months of 1993. You were prepared to concede that that may have occurred with respect to about 200 or 300 Muslims. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't ready to accept it as such. If I recall correctly, I said that it was based on what I heard here. You told me that evidence was heard in the courtroom, and I followed up by saying that based on what I heard in the courtroom, that would be the approximate figure. No one counted them, 150 or so. I really don't know, but I did put the hedge. I can tell you clearly that while I was down there, I never had any information of anyone driving people away while I was commanding from the right bank to the left. I can also say that the efforts we put in, including myself, along the chain of command to educate troops did bear fruit, in spite of grave war conditions, and I know it for certain because I had information showing that, that more than 7.000 Muslims remained on the western side of Mostar throughout the war, and I am proud of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you were to be shown documents, HVO documents, that indicate that there was, in fact, a very dramatic reduction in the number of Muslims living in Mostar during the period of spring to the end of 1993, would that change your view?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what way? If I had known it then or if I learn of that now, what would that change in my view? I was discussing the time while I was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm telling you precisely about what took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's look at a document, then, just to round this off. We have a new one that I believe has been distributed. It's P07500. It is a report on the development trend of expelled persons and refugees in Mostar municipality since the beginning of the homeland war, and it's made by the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees. And it's admitted into evidence. General, what I'd like to do is just to simply take you to one of the tables that are found in this report; namely, it's table number VIII. It's a Roman numeral VIII, on the English version it's page 8 of the English, and on the Croatian version it is on page -- excuse me. General, if you manage to find table 8 in Croatian before I do, let me know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It appears to be on page 7 of the Croatian version. And recognising that this involves some periods of time that precede the time you were commanding the HVO from the 24th of July, if you look in column number 4, table VIII, what you see is that beginning from the 6th of March, 1993, according to these figures, you had 43.464 Muslims in the Mostar municipality, and that by the 23rd of October, you had -- virtually three-quarters of that number was gone and you had 10.548 Muslims living in Mostar, and that figure then remained roughly the same. And so first of all, General, wouldn't it appear that, in fact, there were thousands of Muslims who, for some reason -- perhaps we won't agree on what the reasons were, but for some reason about three-quarters of the Muslim population in Mostar municipality moved away or was no longer present in Mostar by the 23rd of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mathematically speaking, it is correct that 23 per cent out of the figure mentioned on the 6th of March to the 21st of March, 1993, left. Mathematically speaking, that is correct. However, that's all one can conclude from all that, especially if you see that this drastic reduction obviously followed the ABiH attack on the HVO on the 9th of May, 1993. Everything else needs much more thorough research to see whether those people went to Croatia, whether they went to the east bank, and what followed. In any case, the fact that is important is that while I was down there, the figure was not dwindling and there was no mention of any expulsions of Muslims as a phenomenon which could have been structured thinking or effort on the part of the HVO to drive Muslims away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So that, General, I doubt that it would be very productive for us to discuss the reasons behind these numbers, and so I'm not going to go there. But you would agree with me, then, that according to this and based on what you know, there was a very significant drop in the Muslim population of Mostar municipality, and that during the same period of time there was actually an increase in the Croat population, as reflected in column 3 of this table?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment this table, except for the fact that I was familiar with, and that is that the number of Muslims and Serbs remain in the western part of Mostar, and I shared that idea with my soldiers. Otherwise, I can't comment who it was who drafted the table, based on what data, I have absolutely no knowledge about the figures therein. Therefore, I cannot provide either a positive or a negative answer. This goes beyond my knowledge. I shared with you what I knew, and I told you that one really needs to know what the true reasons are for someone to leave; for example, fear of being killed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: I just want to say that the Prosecutor two times make mis-characterisation of document. On page 4, line 15, 16, and page 5, line 7, he mentioned that those data are related to Mostar municipality, which is not the case. It's very clear in both tables on this page that it was said population of Mostar municipality who live under control of HVO. And, second, in next table, also under control of HVO. It does mean that it is not Mostar municipality. Mostar municipality is the area under control of HVO, plus under control of Army of BH, and plus part of municipality under control of Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Praljak, this had not escaped my attention, and I wanted to say something about it. This table is important for the Prosecutor, since it lies at the heart of its case; all the more reason for no one to make a mistake. You do not challenge the figures which are reflected in this table. Everybody factors these in, and these figures come from the HVO. We can see that in the months of March, there are 43.464 Muslims in Mostar, but as Mr. Prlic says, Mostar is under the control of the HVO. In other words, one may imagine that these are the Muslims in West Mostar. And from October onwards, because in May there is no precise data, but in October, when you are in command, as you know, there are 10.548, which means that, in mathematical terms, 30.000 people have left West Mostar. These people have perhaps gone to East Mostar. If they have gone over to East Mostar, these people still remain in Mostar, on the face of it. This table should be compared with a table which was established during the census of 1991, but in 1991 was there a distinction made between East and West Mostar? I doubt that, because the table must have included Mostar municipalities and its neighbourhoods. Therefore, this table needs to be compared with the other one. Whatever the case may be, there is an important piece of information here. Do you agree with the Prosecutor that there are approximately 30.000 Muslims less in Mostar under the control of the HVO? These people have left. We don't know whether they've gone to East Mostar or elsewhere. Can you agree with the Prosecutor on this matter? One moment. I am putting the question to Mr. Praljak, so let him answer. And, Ms. Alaburic, you can take the floor afterwards in order not to take -- not to prompt his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, I simply cannot answer that question by saying I agree or disagree. I see a table before me, much as anyone else in the courtroom. I didn't participate in its drafting. I don't know whether it is true or not. I agree that the figures are as they are on this piece of paper. That's the only thing I can confirm. Secondly, I drafted a document for this Tribunal, and I handed it over. The census was conducted per municipality. I drafted a table showing how many Muslims there were in the 1991 census living in the area of Western Mostar. You can see that precisely, per municipality. And as far as I recall, and I can double-check, perhaps 2.000 Muslims lived in the western part of Mostar, in addition to the figure shown here of 10.000, according to the census in 1991. In any case, I can bring that tomorrow because I still have the tables. I even think that Judge Prandler asked me about that table. I remember that clearly when I was showing it to the Court. So what happened with those refugees who arrived in Mostar in 1992? What happened with them, where they went? Was there an exchange during which the refugees were exchanged for those Croats living on the east bank? How many left elsewhere? All these questions are important, and this is a complex issue. In essence, one needs to know why people left. I know that numerous Croats left both Eastern and Western Mostar in 1992, and many Serbs left as well, but just look at these figures in here. Many of those Muslims who were still in Mostar were protected. Of course, there were individual cases which were resolved differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Judge Antonetti, I believe your question was exceptionally important. In a way, I simply wanted to contribute to a better understanding of this situation. If we equate the right bank of the Neretva River with the territory under control of the HVO, irrespective of the fact that there were parts which were not, then we would have to compare the table at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. For the record, Mr. President, I'm going to object to this sort of intervention which I think is inappropriate during the course of my cross-examination. It's not in response to anything the Trial Chamber said, and it's just commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic -- one moment, Ms. Alaburic. I thank you for having said that my question is an important one, but all the questions I put are important questions. So you are stating the obvious. But I recognise that it is a good thing that Defence counsel think that it is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, one sentence, Your Honour. On the right bank, in 1991, there were a bit over 21.000 Muslims. The table at page 7 that we saw mentions the figure of about 43.000 Muslims, and the 22.000 in excess were not domicile. They arrived in Mostar at some point in time and then possibly proceeded on, looking for a longer-term solution. Therefore, I believe it is completely inappropriate, and this constitutes my objection to Mr. Stringer's question, to use the data of 43.000 Muslims in Western Mostar in 1993, to see all of that population is domicile which, in turn, then left Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Ms. Alaburic, what you were about to say, I was about to say also. Mr. Praljak, if there had been ethnic cleansing, the population in West Mostar amounted to such and such a figure. And if, after that, the Muslim population in Mostar, in West Mostar, amounts to such and such, the difference between the two, let's just say X and Y, could amount to ethnic cleansing if these figures are very high. That is the principle which we put forward. I have studied sciences, and I believe that you can only agree with me. Now, to understand clearly what is happening here, it is important to know, before the events occurred, what this first figure X was. You said that you had prepared a table which, according to you at the time, this X amounted to 12.000, and then if the X amounted to 12.000 in the month of October, we have the figure of 10.540, so there would be a decrease of 1.500 people. Now, Ms. Alaburic stated this, but I was about to say so. The 40.000 in the month of March amount to the Muslim population that come from East Mostar, in addition to refugees who aggregated the figures and were added to the Muslims already there either because of the Serb offensive or for other reasons, and this figure of 40.000 did not amount to 40.000 Muslims at the time. Do you agree with me here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that for certain, Your Honour. I prepared the tables, and I can have them here for you tomorrow. Therefore, there is a difference between these two tables, too. In table II, it says the right bank of the Neretva, which includes, I believe, Jasenica and Krusevo areas outside Mostar. The second table speaks only of the right side of Mostar. One needs to be very precise. I think I remember well that there were some 12.000 domicile Muslims in the area of Mostar in 1991, in the part which later fell under the control of the HVO. I wanted to make that calculation to show how many of those Muslims, against the thesis proposed by the Prosecutor, would no longer be there in the later years. We have shown here several times that the 30.000 refugees in 1992 arrived in the area of Mostar. I showed you precise tables and where they came from. And after that, there was movement en masse. Half a million of them ended up in Croatia, in Brela, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the case may be, I remember that evidence was shown on the number of dead people. The Trial Chamber will, therefore, purposefully look into the figures of dead people in 1991 and the number of dead people, i.e., Muslims, in 1993. If the number of dead people is the same, this may prove that the population figures remain unchanged. If there's an important decrease in the number, then something has most likely occurred. So we have a whole series of data which help us understand the situation better. That said, Mr. Stringer, you have the floor again. You can, of course, if you so wish, go into greater detail in all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I want to acknowledge that Dr. Prlic was absolutely correct in pointing out that the table relates only to the HVO-controlled parts of Mostar, and that's certainly a significant factor. And the Trial Chamber, I think, will draw its own conclusions about what that means in terms of the Prosecution's submissions on what happened in Mostar, in terms of the Muslim population, both the refugees and people who'd always been living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to maybe continue a little bit with this, because it does -- there are parts of this that do relate to some of our discussions even, I think, from yesterday and the day before, when we were talking about demographics and your own testimony about wishing to establish an autonomous Croat area with absolute and relative majorities of Croat people. If you look at the text that's just above table number VIII. Table number VIII is the table that we've been looking at here, and if you look at the text -- if you read the text that just precedes that table, so if you want to go to the previous page, I'll read part of that to you and then ask you some questions. They say: "We consider it necessary to emphasise that according to the last census statistics, 12.654 of the inhabitants of Mostar municipality, as a whole, declared themselves as Yugoslavs. We may assert that the largest number of these are Muslims and Serbs, while Croats make up only an insignificant part of this figure." I'll skip the next sentence, and then it continues: "In the near future, in the next census, under conditions of democracy and pluralism, it is very likely that the majority of Yugoslavs will declare themselves according to the nation to which they previously belonged. Should this prediction come true, and it is very likely that it will, Croats would then become a minority people in the town of Mostar. For this not to become a reality, it is necessary today, if today is not already too late, to seriously begin thinking about and taking all civilised measures to see that Croats do not move away from the town and rural parts of the municipality, but rather keep living here in the capital of their state in Mostar and Mostar municipality, and all the one-time parts of that municipality which the former Communist, anti-Croatian authorities administratively divided from Mostar." And then the text continues on, General, with a discussion of the - and I know that you've talked about this in the past - earlier changes to the municipal borders which, in your view, were done in order to make Croats a minority, and so the text goes on to discuss those -- what basically is the view that you've expressed, that the borders were gerrymandered, if you will, in order to put Croats in the minority there. I'm more interested in the text that precedes that, obviously, that raises two questions that relate to our previous discussion on this issue, because I asked you, I think it was yesterday, whether, in fact, your vision of this autonomous Croat area, where Croats would be in the majority, whether your own vision really required that there be a control over the demographics in order to enable Croats to maintain those majorities. And, in fact, here in the early part of 1994, in this Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we're seeing just that, aren't we? We're seeing, as a matter of policy -- or at least it's being suggested that the policy be undertaken to, at the very least, facilitate the maintenance of a Croat majority that prevails in Mostar at this time. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you have been stating things for a page -- for a whole page now. You started off by saying that I said somewhere that I want to round off an area. There was some thesis of yours someplace which I've already forgotten. In any case, I disagree with it, and please do not put words in my mouth. Furthermore, I know, Mr. Stringer, that during the Communist regime in the former Yugoslavia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipalities were drawn, or their boundaries, so as to have a Serb majority in such areas in which, under normal circumstances, they wouldn't have one. In Mostar, this includes the areas -- excuse me. Your question was a page long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying about the previous changes to the borders, and maybe you misunderstood me, because I was trying simply to observe that some of the views expressed in this text are very similar, I believe, to the views you've expressed on this -- on this issue of changing borders to create Croat minorities, and so I don't think it's necessary for us to talk about that again. You've already talked about it in the past, and we understand that's the position. I'm trying to focus on a different issue, which is the objective that's indicated here of maintaining what is now a Croat majority in Mostar, by whatever means, whether that would involve changing borders, municipal borders, or restoring previous municipal borders, or undertaking other policies. My point that I'm putting to you is this: The fact is that this sort of demographic engineering is necessary in order to maintain the Croat majorities that you envisioned for this autonomous Croat area that you've been telling us about; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I have to raise an objection. At page 14, line 15, Mr. Stringer has just introduced a new category, "by whatever means." I think what the document actually states is "by civilised means." It reads "by whatever means." That is not exactly what the text says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam. Of course, I have noticed that. This is a vulgar and crude insinuation. You may be the Prosecutor, but you are not God. You are simply making things up as you go along, and you have no right to do that. It reads here "by civilised means." That's the first thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stringer may have innocently used some words without seeing a problem to that, so before he answers the objection, you are taking the floor immediately and you're attacking him. Wait for him to answer and to state what was really on his mind. Even sometimes Judges, you know, are called upon, they wanted to say something, and counsel is going to misunderstand them, and then there's going to be a huge -- you're making a problem out of nothing. So just wait for the person challenged to explain himself, say, This is what exactly I meant, rather than attacking him directly, saying, You're a prosecutor. You're doing anything and everything. Please let Mr. Stringer explain what he actually had on his mind. Mr. Stringer, an objection was made. Could you please answer it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for allowing me to respond. No, I didn't mean to imply that by this late period of time there was going to be some policy of forcibly evicting non-Croats in order to maintain a Croat majority. By -- when I said "whatever means," I was simply, in my own mind, referring to the suggestion that there need to be policies in place for keeping Croats. Now, they said "civilised policies," and I certainly accept that because that's what the text says. So I didn't mean to imply that anything violent or vile was necessarily being contemplated by this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's just -- it's simply the point I'm trying to make, General, is here we are, we're very late in the conflict, we're actually getting close to the end of the conflict between the Croats -- I should say the ABiH and the HVO at the time this report is made in early 1994. The point I'm making is that in order to establish and maintain this autonomous Croat area, and I put this to you earlier, it's necessary to control demographics, and so what I'm putting to you now is this: Aren't we seeing just that, when we have people writing reports now keeping track of the ethnic compositions and recommending policy as a way of maintaining a particular demographic profile? Isn't this exactly consistent with what I was putting to you earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'll try to be as calm about this as possible. You did say "by whatever means," which is something that we don't come across anywhere in this document. That appears to be your position, however. "By whatever means," would mean exactly what it says in any language, "by whatever means." That's not true. I can't find that anywhere in this document. Further on, you go on to say "by various policies," or "by political means." Well, hold on a minute there, please ask me the question then. You can't -- Mr. Stringer, you can't toy around with me and stage these soliloquies of yours. Please ask the question. I do not agree with anything that you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, let me take the floor, because in the Rules, Judges are here to control how witnesses are questioned. Mr. Stringer was asking you a very simple question. Any child could put this question to you. He's saying, given the demographic situation as it was, where, according to what he says, Croats were a minority, don't you think that the HVO wanted to control this trend by making sure that they would have control over demography through different means, means such as the ones that are spelled out in the document, civilised means? This is exactly what he wants to know. It's a very clear question, so please tell him what your opinion on this is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion on this problem is as follows: The Croats constituted a majority or were on their way to becoming a majority. By changing the borders within Mostar city, they became a small minority. This was a practice that one had to fight because it was an evil practice of suppressing people. I knew that at the time; I know it now. I stood up against it then, and I stand against it today. Secondly, one must employ any civilised means - civilised means, I say - to keep the number of Croats throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina from being reduced. One must employ any civilised means, including preventing any draining of capital, workers from abroad being brought in, and I can talk about this for hours, the foreign currency being brought into Bosnia-Herzegovina by workers from abroad. This is still 2 million German marks, but the exchange rate between the dinar and the mark was very poor, unfavorable. No one was allowed to open any production lines over there, that there was a lot of political persecution, and every time there was a census it would turn out that the Croats now numbered 2 per cent or 3 per cent less than in the previous ones. One must employ any political means to fight the Communist state, as it was then, and I would still say that even today we should employ any civilised means to keep the existing Croat majorities in these territories which they have now inhabited for over 800 years. I'm not saying "by whatever means," however. What I am saying is "by civilised means."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, there's something I don't understand in what you're saying. You're saying that the Croats were a majority. Fine. Well, I feel that according to this census, the Croats were a minority. Okay. Now, you're saying they changed the borders of the town. It's line 13, page 17. They changed the borders. When was it? During the Communist regime; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three major villages, Ljuti Dolac, Tepcici, Polog, were thrown out, thereby altering the ethnic make-up of the city itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. What's important for us, as Judges, is to know exactly what prevailed in 1992, as of October, in Mostar. Could you tell us whether, in October, in Mostar, the Croats were a majority? That's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In October 1992, the Mostar city municipality was established in a perfectly regular way, and the Croats constituted a majority, if we don't take into account the refugees coming in at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're saying that in October 1992, the situation is such that Croats constituted a majority, unless if you take into account the influx of Muslim refugees, which changed the figures. Very well. I'm trying to find my way through this flood of elements and figures and facts in order to really understand what you're telling us. Mr. Stringer, I will give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The only -- the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. If I may just say a word or two. I tried not to intervene before the question was asked, but there's one thing that I'd like to point out for the benefit of the record. The Prosecutor starts with his question at page 13, line 16, and actually what the Prosecutor is doing there is putting forward his theory that this was a question of an HZ-HB policy, an HZ-HB policy. Their policy was, he said, and he did correct himself later on, to take any civilised measures they could to preserve the ethnic make-up. He's asking this question based on this document. If we take a closer look at this document, who it was produced by, first of all, the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons of HZ-HB in Mostar, what I would say is that this is a very small administrative unit. This is certainly not the political power within the HZ-HB. This is just an office that does administrative work. As anywhere else in the world, it is not an executive office and it does not devise policy. What this office does is produce a report, because that's what this document is called, a report. This is a simple matter of providing information, and it's signed by two persons. The report deals with facts and makes these known facts available, and so on and so forth. And there is a particular reference that my learned friend has drawn our attention to. All those people involved in this task make the following suggestion. Some demographic policies might be devised, but only by civilised means. But this is not an HZ-HB policy, so it's erroneous on the part of the OTP. Please, Your Honours, allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I think it's not proper, Mr. Kovacic. You are just pleading. You're giving arguments on this. You are discussing the substance. You have the opportunity of doing that in redirect and mainly in the pleadings, but I think now we are in question and answers to the witness, full stop. And we must end this bad habit, which is not in line with the basic procedural rules and customs, to start discussing here. This is not the moment where issues are discussed, and you were discussing issues now, as others have before. I have not intervened, I admit to that, but I think that we should let Mr. Stringer to go forward. We'll never get anywhere if we start now having pleading sessions in between the hearing of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, if I may, if I may. Maybe I wasn't clear, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Kovacic. I fully support what my fellow Judge just said, but I also want to add something. I believe that what you just said is something you've already said earlier. Earlier, you already said that those who were making reports were civil servants, do not embody policies, as such. You already told us all this months ago. This is no surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. In my desire to cut this short, I may have been less than specific. I was just trying to argue my own objection to the way the question was phrased. The question must not be allowed, because the Prosecutor is by asking this implying -- or, rather, in his question he is clearly suggesting that there was something, and I'm not going into what, was a policy pursued by the HZ-HB, regardless of what exactly. I'm objecting to that question. Why? Because that does not follow from the document. I want to round this off by saying the following: A large part of this whole discussion is headed that way: Was this a policy, was this not a policy? What sort of demographic policy, civilised, not civilised, permitted or not permitted? Simply because the question was erroneously phrased. This is a question that must not be allowed. This is not an HZ-HB policy, and that is certainly not something that the document suggests. If the Prosecutor believes so, perhaps they should bring up a document that is politically natured, but this one isn't, and that much is clear. That's why I have to argue my objection. The question must not be allowed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it to you, General, and in fact if it's not been stated clearly earlier in my cross-examination, I'll directly put it to you now. In order to maintain these Croat majorities, whether absolute or relative, for this autonomous Croatian area that you were fighting for, the fact is that it would be and it was, in fact, HVO/HZ-HB policy to control the demographics, to increase Croat populations in these areas while at the same time diminishing non-Croat populations; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. These are insinuations. That's not true. I don't know whether they ever drew up a document that -- what you're suggesting is not true. Quite the contrary, in fact. In 1992 and 1993, a large number of Croats left Mostar for Croatia. They fled. They were afraid. Many of them had been killed. You know, Mr. Stringer, this was a matter of life and death, and death is an unnatural occurrence. Many people are afraid of dying, and that's why they were leaving. Both groups, in fact, fleeing, if you like, which is only natural. I can, however, give you my opinion. Personally, I would have committed myself to a policy to use any civilised means available to keep the numbers of Croats across Bosnia and Herzegovina from being reduced, any civilised means available. That's my position, if you want to know. And there were certain injustices that had to be redressed, injustices which had led to the numbers of the Croats decreasing year in and year out. That was my nationalist, if you like, Croat policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But the fact is that from November of 1991, when Mostar was declared to be the capital of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it was absolutely imperative, if Mostar is going to be the capital of this Croatian Community, that it be a town or a municipality where, in fact, Croats were in a majority, and they needed to recover any earlier majorities that they had. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would that be crucial? We were talking about regions. When Mostar was declared to be the capital, that was something which was in keeping with the guide-lines provided by the international community. The same thing applies to all those Croats remaining in other areas. Nothing about achieving that objective was bad or under-hand, nor, indeed, were any under-hand means used in the process. Mostar did not necessarily have to be a majority city. It was a Croat majority city, but some things had been done in a way that wasn't good previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question. Mr. Praljak, you have said, and this is still page 22, line 16, just disappearing, that between -- in 1992 and 1993, Croats left Mostar. If I look at table VIII, I see, for 6 March 1993, 29.105 Croats, and then for 11 December of the same year, 35.968. I find it difficult to interpret this as a reduction, so it seems to be in contradiction to what you have just declared. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no contradiction, Judge Trechsel. In 1992, Croats were leaving Mostar in considerable numbers. You remember those buses and all the children leaving, people moving out. Nevertheless, this information is from October --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please stick to the question. The question relates to 1993. You have said 1992 and 1993, and my observation and question relates to 1993. So, please, don't go into 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Judge Trechsel, it's impossible to answer your question unless we take into account what was going on in the actual war at the time. You want to reduce things to a model that simply doesn't make sense. At first, the Croats were leaving Mostar, and then there were other areas from which they had been expelled. They were coming in -- well, listen, you can't make me, you can't make me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I note you do not answer the question, and that's it. Mr. Stringer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer makes -- your question makes no sense at all. It is a static question. It is not a question which takes into account the dynamics of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are here as a witness. It's impertinent and contemptuous of Judges for you to criticise their questions in this way. So you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- have to answer the questions of the Prosecutor. That is your role, and you have not to teach us what your role is. If at all, it's vice versa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not trying to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, don't shout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't yell at me. I'm not -- no, all I'm telling you is don't yell at me. I'm not some servant of yours, and I'm certainly not a thing just sitting here. I'm talking about your question, not about your person. In my opinion, your question makes no sense. If that's what I think, I'm going to say it as well. You are an honourable person, but your question may or may not be one that lends itself to a reasonable answer. I respect you, but it doesn't depend on the actual person. When I notice a question that isn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Listen to us. You are going to be the laughing stock of this Tribunal if you are continuing this way. You are a witness. Your role is very clear. You undertook an oath, and you are -- you have to do whatever the Rules prescribe for you to do so. And that is why I really ask you to stop this pleading, to stop this discussion. It is not a debating club here, it is a tribunal, and I believe that it is high time that everybody would take this into account. So let us proceed. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that as my fellow Judges are taking the floor, I also must take the floor. Mr. Praljak, you are here to answer the questions put to you. It might that sometimes -- you know, that when I am putting a question to you, if I make a -- I always tell you if I'm wrong, please correct me. I always say that. But the Prosecutor's time is precious. He has an allotted time to put questions to you, you know, and the time for the questions and the answers are deducted from his whole time. So if you're making pleadings during your answers, then the Prosecutor will not be happy with that, and of course he will say so. When Judges are putting a question to you, you might think that maybe the Judge is wrong in putting this question, or maybe put a wrong question to you, and then you can say, Well, for this year, I can't answer, but for another year, I may. But don't reformulate the question. Yesterday, we saw a video, and I wanted to take the floor, but I decided not to. But I thought over it, I thought about it overnight, and I believe that I absolutely must talk to you about it. The Prosecutor asked you a series of questions from this video, and they were essential questions. Everyone understood that, and you understood it very well also. At one point in time, there was a Catholic priest making a speech to the soldiers on this video, and I wondered about this. I said this is quite surprising, to have a Catholic priest speaking to soldiers, notably if Mr. Praljak had come in order to spell the good words from Zagreb, as the Prosecutor put it to you. I believe that this would have deserved a few words from you. You should have explained the role of the Catholic clergy in all this. You should have explained -- you might have explained what this priest was there for. You said it was -- according to you, it was a mistake or an error, but you didn't really explain why he was here. So there are some very important moments where you must take the floor and explain, but sometimes you just decide to take the floor at any moment, and there you might irritate those listening to you. Another example. Yesterday, you told us about the 30 weddings with the Libyans, and my fellow Judge took the floor and said, This is totally irrelevant. While you mentioned it, and probably because you had a good reason for that, but you mentioned it because you said, This was the -- this corresponds to the situation I expected. Well, the fact is that we don't know what the situation is today. The Trial Chamber went to Mostar once with the counsels. We saw the sites, we toured the sites, but we did not analyse the political situation prevailing in 2007, 2008, or 2009. So when you're telling us that this situation corresponds to what you expected, this leaves us in the dark. This doesn't provide us with anything, and this is totally irrelevant for us, at least on the face of it. It might have some relevance, but then you have to explain and demonstrate what you meant, saying that, What is happening is Islamisation and that in 1992 and 1993, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was what was happening through the imams and the Mujahedins and so on, but you didn't say that. So you're trying to make speeches, you're trying to plead, but you're handicapping yourself, because there were some elements that you could highlight, and you don't do that, and, on the other hand, you irritate everyone. So, please, listen to the questions carefully. Mr. Stringer is doing his job perfectly. He's putting very clear questions, in a very quiet fashion. So listen to the question, think about it, and answer very coolly to the question. If you want to add anything, you know that there is redirect, and you have excellent counsels. They're listening to all this, and they will put these questions to you later on. There's no need for speeches, because your counsels are there, you know, to put these questions to you later on in the redirect. Please do not -- please answer the question precisely. It will be more effective. If there's anything you want to develop, you can tell Mr. Stringer, I can answer you by yes or no, but if you wish, I may expound on this. And he might say, Yes, do so, or, Don't. Because as my colleague -- my fellow Judge Trechsel said, you are now in the space where you totally belong to the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor is in charge of his cross-examination, and you're here to answer his questions, and only that. I hope you understand what I'm saying. This is in your interest. Mr. Stringer, please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, on this -- maybe the discussion has evolved to a place where it would be useful for us to go back to one of the exhibits from yesterday, and so it might not be one that everybody has with them in the courtroom because it was at the very end of the previous binder. It was the census data that we were looking at a little bit -- I think that was yesterday. P10519. And even if we don't have it in the courtroom, I think in e-court, if we could just simply put up the data, the census data for the Mostar municipality, which is on page 9 of the document. And if they could just blow that up, maybe we can all look at those numbers on the screen and work from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Mr. Stringer to provide the general with the binders. Yesterday, all of the documents were taken away from him. Therefore, now he cannot make use of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You took the documents away yesterday, Mr. Stringer. Perhaps it would be a good idea for me to have them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If it's still in the courtroom, we can give it to the general. I can give him my page, just to move this along faster. It's just simply the Mostar numbers that I'm interested in. I can give the general mine, and I can just look off the screen. I'll work off the screen, if my eyes are good enough. Okay, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, my learned friend is more than welcome to have our hard copy. It may facilitate matters and make it a little bit easier on his very young eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I appreciate counsel's offer. They've blown it up on the screen, and this is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just a couple questions on this, because you've been talking about this -- the reduction or the departure of Croats. And I think it's worth noting here, recognising that these figures go back only about 20 or 22 years from the time of the conflict, but if you at least -- if you look at the Mostar municipality, in fact, what you see is, would you agree with me, first of all, as between Croats, Muslims, and Serbs, pretty consistent -- pretty static numbers, not a lot of change in any direction among any of the three groups? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The figures are increasing; 32.000, 36.000. So there was this natural growth of the population, and a number of people arrived as well since at that time Mostar became a university centre with schools, hospitals, et cetera. There were many things taking place in the meantime, but that would take away our time if I started discussing them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sure. You correctly note that the overall population does increase from about 90.000, in 1971, to over 126.000 in 1991. I'm more interested in the percentages, because it looks to me as though the Croats and the Muslims are very close throughout this entire 20-year period, both of them sort of hovering around the mid 30s, in terms of the percentage of the overall population. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of percentages, that would be approximately so. There were more or less the same numbers of Croats and Muslims in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you've talked about the departure of Croats, and there is a -- about three percentage points reduction in the Croat portion from 1971 to 1981, I notice, going from 36.6 down to 33.5 per cent. But would you agree with me, General, that this shows that during the same period, there was actually almost twice as much of a reduction in the Muslim numbers? The Muslims were also leaving Mostar during that 10-year period, going down to 31 per cent of the population from 37. Actually, more Muslims were present, but their overall percentage of the population went down by over 6 per cent; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the Muslims increased in number by some 10.000, and the percentage went from 37 to 34 per cent. As far as I can do my math, I believe that's 3 per cent less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, I was looking at Croats and Muslims both for the 10 years from 1971 to 1981, and during that period both of them went down, in terms of percentage. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of percentages, yes. The absolute figures were increased, but in terms of percentages, that was reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then finally for the period of 1981 to 1991, and I know that you challenge the census figures for 1991, but again this would indicate that we have roughly an equality as between the Muslims and the Croats, and we've had roughly an equality in percentage throughout this entire 20-year period; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for 1991, that census, as I said, is not legally valid because the census procedure was not completed, and there are some other reasons why I see it as untrue. As for the other part of your assertion, I wouldn't agree with that. There are small changes, in terms of percentages, but it's only by a few points of inhabitants increasing or numbers going down. Let's not see this in any philosophical way. These are simple figures, indicating simple things. As to the reduction of the number of Croats, I wasn't talking only about Mostar, which is rather specific. I was discussing this occurrence at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. There were significant numbers of Croats departing abroad to work. If, say, 10 per cent of Croats, 100 thousand Croats go to work abroad, then that would represent 11 per cent of the entire Croat population. But when 100 thousand out of 2.4 million Muslims go to work abroad, then that is 3.5 per cent or 3 per cent of the population, and so on... This is a bit more complicated than we are trying to explain. Unfortunately, I don't want to take this any further, although it does require further attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And perhaps to try to round this off and to bring it back to the original exhibit, which was P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. Still looking at the same table, Mr. Praljak, we see the figure of 12.768, which amounts to 10 per cent. Is this a figure which coincides with the people that declared themselves Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The 12.760 that declare themselves Yugoslavs, according to the document we saw a while ago, this document which gave rise to a lot of reactions, P7500, there's a slight mistake because the authors who were supposed to turn this into a book say that there were 12.650, whereas here we have 12.760. The figures don't tally. But out of these 12.768, if the majority are Muslim, 34.6 of them or 34 per cent of them could very easily increase, and then the Croats are in the minority. What do you have to say to this, excluding all passion and exchange of views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of people who declare themselves Yugoslavs, as you can see, changed depending on the current political propaganda. People were encouraged to declare themselves Yugoslavs. So as you can see, in 1981 the figure rose from 2.000 to 16.000 later in 1991, and then the figure went down, and later on they almost completely disappeared, they were left in negligible numbers. This was an attempt of the Communist ideology to come up with a completely new nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you're not answering my question. In mathematical terms, the fact that out of 12.768, a majority would be Muslim, in that case these Muslims must be added on to the 34 per cent, and therefore, in Mostar in 1991, the majority is a Muslim majority, not a Croatian majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no evidence that among these 12.768 there were mostly Muslims. There is no proof of that whatsoever. Actually, quite the contrary, I assert that a lot of people who were in mixed marriages, who originally were Croats, then declared themselves Yugoslav, because the most difficult thing there was to be a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the case may be, you and your counsel, you will have time to read this report again. But the authors of the report say, and this is black on white, and they say that the greatest number are Muslims and Serbs, whereas the Croats constitute an insignificant part. This is what is stated here. This is what they both say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I did see that, but I don't agree with their interpretation. They are not putting forth a single scientific argument for their assertion. This is an arbitrary argument. I am familiar with such ideas, and I can pretty much guarantee you that it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You, in fact, anticipated my next question on this, which was to factor in this -- the figures on the Yugoslavs, so I don't think I need to follow up on that. And after nearly the first session, I think I'm ready to actually go back to the HVO structure issues that we -- that we were talking about yesterday. So, General, I see you don't have the binder in front of you from yesterday. It is the binder that is the big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wouldn't it be a good idea, then, to have the break now? I think it's probably better to have the break now, and then we shall get back to that binder. Right, we shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I see that you've been handed the binder of the current set of documents we're going to be talking about. Before we get into the binder again today, you'll recall from yesterday I was asking you about various units within the HVO structure or where they might fall within that structure you. Do you recall that, in general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And one aspect of that that I want to spend a little bit of time on now relates to a gentleman named Mladen Naletilic, whose nickname or his nom de guerre was Tuta. You've mentioned him already in your testimony, particularly in connection with a meeting that occurred, I believe, on the 9th or 10th of May, 1993. Perhaps you could clarify again for us the date of that meeting with Mr. Tuta.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 11th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the 26th --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it wasn't a meeting with Mr. Naletilic. I came to attend a meeting, a separate meeting. Hence, it wasn't a meeting with him. He was just present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. I understand that, and I recall that at least part of your testimony about the meeting was given in private session. So we have your testimony on that, and I'm not going to ask you about that at this point. I do want to take you back to your testimony of 26 May, in this case, 26 May of 2009. And Judge Antonetti asked you, and this is page 40761 of the transcript, Judge Antonetti asked you: "Mr. Praljak, since you mentioned the functions of the different people, could you please tell me exactly what was Mr. Naletilic's position?" And your answer was: "No, I cannot. I have no idea what his function in the HVO was, and in -- in what capacity he was there, I don't know that, either." Do you recall that testimony, General? Is that still your position in respect of Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall having said that, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that testimony, where you said you don't know what his title is -- his function was, you say you don't know what his function in the HVO was or what capacity he was there, does that apply to all periods during 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question completely. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to distinguish between the period of time when you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff and the period of time before you were commander of the HVO Main Staff. And so when you told the Trial Chamber that you did not know what Mr. Naletilic's function was, are you referring to the period that you were the commander of the Main Staff, or to the period of time prior to your command of the Main Staff, or were you talking about both of those periods of time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before that, I didn't know his exact function. I did know he had a unit of his. And as far as my information went, at the beginning until mid-1993 or, to be more precise, until May 1993 -- well, in any case, I can't answer your question precisely. I didn't know what his function or position was throughout that period. Anything I say would be speculation. I simply didn't have the facts pertaining to his position within the HVO. As I said, during the time I was in command, I had no command over him and I did not contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, did command soldiers who fought as part of the HVO armed forces? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a degree of certainty, I could tell you that his units, in 1992, fought as part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, now, when you say "1992," I think it's important for us to distinguish which conflict. Are you now referring to the operations which led to the liberation of Mostar and the defeat, if you will, of the Serb forces there in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, that's what I had in mind, the operation organised by that unit. It was the liberation of Orlovac in 1992. That was the beginning of the process of liberation of the right bank of the Neretva, and following that I assumed command of the whole operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, for the purposes of our discussion now about Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, I'd like to restrict that to the period that begins in, let's say, October of 1992, just prior to the conflict breaking out in Prozor, and then the period of time that follows -- the months that follow until the time you left the HVO Main Staff in November of 1993. Okay? So I'd like for our discussion about Mr. Tuta to be restricted to the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH. Okay?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put your questions, and I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if -- I'll tell you specifically if I'm referring to the prior period of time during the summer of 1992. So, again, just to clarify that, your testimony that you didn't know what Mr. Naletilic's function was, are you saying that you didn't know what his function was during the entire period of the HVO-ABiH conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of function is something I've already answered. I didn't know his function. I did know, however, in 1992 that he commanded a unit, and I told you precisely that that unit participated in the liberation of Orlovac, where I was present. They prepared it. They came to see me and asked me about certain things. And if you're asking me about the places where I was, that I can answer, to the extent of what I know about such things. We have to bear in mind what my functions were at each period of time and what was my reason for coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: From October of 1992 until the 9th of November, 1993, is it true that Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was in command of soldiers who fought as part of the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've already answered that question. As of October 1992, I simply don't have any knowledge about it because I held no position at that time. But as of the moment I took over command, I have explained that to you, and there's nothing further to add. You can put the question as many times as you like and I'll always answer the same. How can I discuss this period in 1992 and 1993 when I became commander on the 24th of July? And in the meantime when I was there, I was busy with some completely different things. First and foremost, I was trying to bring the conflict under some kind of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: From the period of time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, 24 July 1993, until the 9th of November, 1993, did Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, command soldiers who fought as part of the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I did not command Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta. As to whether he had units and what sort of units these were, that is something I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your testimony, General, is that during the period of time that you were the highest-ranking military officer of the HVO armed forces, occupying the position of commander of the HVO Main Staff, you're telling us you do not know whether Mladen Naletilic was in command of soldiers who formed a part of your HVO? That seems hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I had asked a question earlier and you did not answer it at the time. And justly so, the Prosecutor is coming back to this. Something that escaped me, but I note that on paragraph 36 of the summary read by the Judges during the Naletilic judgement, the following was said, and it's public. I think I can read it. This is a public judgement. Listen carefully. Tuta was a close friend and a collaborator of Gojko Susak, minister of defence, and thanks to this he had access to President Franjo Tudjman. He was connected to Mate Boban, president of HDZ in BH. And this had escaped me, but it seems that Mr. Naletilic was a friend of Mr. Susak. You were also a friend of Mr. Susak. Are you telling us that you never met Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the incident on the 11th of May, 1993, I hadn't met him again for at least a year. We would need to go into private session for this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the reason you don't want to associate yourself with Mladen Naletilic is because he and his units committed crimes during HVO operations in Sovici/Doljani in April 1993, they were actively involved in the expulsion and the arrests of Muslims in Mostar, beginning on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, and in addition, he and his units fought as part of an HVO operation in Rastani in August of 1993 in which war crimes were committed. Isn't that true, and isn't that the reason why you don't want to associate yourself with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the reason. Were the crimes committed in Sovici? That was up to the Court to establish. I had no knowledge of the crimes at the time. Were there crimes that were committed in Rastani? That is what you say. I have no information indicating that. I don't think any crimes were committed. Based on everything that I knew at the time, it was a militarily-legitimate operation. I do not know whether any of his units were involved in that. It wasn't that simple, really. There was some units that called themselves the Tutici, or something like that, but there is a confusion in terms there. I said that units changed, people came and went. It's not as simple as all that. I can certainly say that I had no knowledge of any crimes that were committed during the war. It's not that I hadn't heard, but in order to legally establish who the perpetrators were, and in what way, that is not the kind of knowledge that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What crimes did you hear of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the crimes that simply -- this man was killed or that man was killed, and then there was an investigation that was launched. So, please, don't, Mr. Stringer. Of course, one hears things like that, a man was killed, a house was set on fire, and it's all investigated. But the fact that you hear of a crime does not mean you can do anything else but make sure an investigation is launched according to a certain set of rules that apply, regardless of the fact of how difficult this actually was at the time, what the town -- what the times were like, what the means were for doing this available to us, and what sort of personnel we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically, General, what are the crimes you're referring to committed by Naletilic or his units, and where did those take place, and when or how did you order that an investigation be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are perverting entirely the meaning of what I told you. What I said is they were not under my command, I had not heard of them specifically committing any crime. Based on the documents that I tendered, when I was there, when I was present, or when I heard that someone had committed an infraction or whatever, I always wanted that person's name. I ordered that this person be seized, thrown into jail, and investigated. What you're saying is not something that I said. You are putting words into my mouth. I never said a single word about this. Quite the contrary, in fact, I'm claiming that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm looking at the bottom of page 41 line 23, and you say just now: "I can certainly say that I had no knowledge of any crimes that were committed during the war. It's not that I hadn't heard. But in order to legally establish who the perpetrators were and in what way, that is not the kind of knowledge that I had." So I'm asking you to specify for us, what are the crimes that you heard about? When did they take place, where? You mentioned that some men were killed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you expecting me after all these years, 20 years, to remember that I had heard about a house being set alight in Prozor or something like that, whatever? Please, don't, don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you've mentioned Prozor, and we're talking about Mladen Naletilic. Is it true that Naletilic or members of -- or his subordinates were present in Prozor, taking part in any HVO operations in that area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At any time from October 1992 until 9 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. I do remember one incident, or more than one, described in the document in quite specific terms. If you can hand the document back to me, and I believe it's an exhibit before this Trial Chamber, I can tell you more about it. During my time as commander there, then I was spending the best part of my time in that area, there were no units that were in any way related to Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The operation in Rastani on the 24th of August, 1993, took place while you were commander of the HVO Main Staff. After that operation -- well, let me ask you this: Were you aware -- did you order that operation to take place, taking Rastani on the 24th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the operation. I think I appointed its commander, in fact, telling him to liberate Rastani, which constituted a grave danger in terms of disrupting the whole front-line around Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you're aware, sir, that war crimes were committed by HVO soldiers, particularly subordinates of Tuta, during that operation? Did you at any time become aware that war crimes were committed in that operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're claiming that war crimes were committed. I had not heard about those, and I have not seen a shred of relevant evidence to the effect that crimes were, in fact, committed. It was a well-defended settlement, well defended. Attacks were launched against the HVO from it. There was a danger that a military operation might be launched, so the decision that I took at the time still strikes me as logical and justified. I had not heard of a single crime. I had not received any reports indicating that crimes had been committed. I am, as yet, still unaware of any judgement or conviction that indicates that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- except for your own claim, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know where the offices of the Defence Department were located in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, well, I can't remember specifically. I can't claim that I wasn't there. I may have been there once, but I can't remember a single time that I went there during my time as commander, the simple reason being I would spend 20 hours a day on the ground, trying to exercise control over our lads in a bid to ward off the offensive that had been going on for 85 days at a stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Naletilic was acting as a security adviser to Bruno Stojic and that he had an office in the Defence Department in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, page 14800, the testimony of Josip Praljak on the 27th of February, 2007, line 11, and we can talk about the time-frame. We'll get to the time-frame with some documents. He says: "At the time, I considered that Bruno Stojic was the president of the office and that Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was an adviser to Mr. Bruno Stojic for security matters." "For security matters." Did you know that to be the case, General, at any time from October of 1992 to November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question. I had no knowledge of that at all, not at the time, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Josip Praljak said that when you enter the building, and this is where the Defence Department is located, on that first floor, on the right-hand side was Mr. Bruno Stojic's office, and straight from the stairs on there was the office of Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta. They were next to each other. Now, did you see Mr. Naletilic's office there at the time you went to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I try to imagine the location of this office if all we have is Mr. Josip Praljak's word? Nor, indeed, do I wish to even try. You asked Josip Praljak, and he answered what he answered. We can just stick to that, because I know nothing about that. I don't think I even went there during my time as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this testimony of Josip Praljak relates to a report he made, and it's Exhibit P06170, which is in your binder, General. If you could take a look at that document, that will give us the time-frame that he's talking about. Mr. President, I think the general needs to take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the meantime, Mr. Stringer, can I ask you in which binder we can find this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's in the first of the two binders that were just most recently distributed. It's the one that says "Binder 1 of 2." It's the larger binder, list 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take the opportunity to put a question to Mr. Prlic. Mr. Prlic, I am currently reading the report which you prepared, which has not been admitted into evidence. On a personal note, I would like you to know this is an assumption, of course. If the Trial Chamber were to decide to hear you as a witness, would you accept to testify as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before he answers that question, I must advise the Trial Chamber that he has a lawyer representing him, and -- he's got two lawyers, in fact, and all questions of that nature should be posed to the lawyers and not to the client. And I regret to have to make this observation, but I do believe that I'm not here sitting as a potted plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a personal question I was putting. Mr. Prlic, before you answer my question, you can seek advice from your counsel. You have told us that you were representing yourself, in part. This is why I have put this question to you. But in light of Mr. Karnavas' comment, you can say that you would like to talk to him about it first and not reply straight away. This is not that urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I must advise, either we withdraw from the case, and I would be perfectly happy to pack my bag and walk out this courtroom this instance, or we adhere to the Rules. He is represented by counsel. Until such time as I am relieved as counsel, I will not allow my client to directly answer such questions posed to him. That's my position. Now, as far as him taking the stand and acting as a witness, at this stage of the game, I must also advise the Trial Chamber that I had specifically asked for a certain amount of time. You, in your collective wisdom, refused - I underscore that word - refused to give us the allotted time necessary for us to put on a defence. You then went on, Mr. President, to say at one point, that had you been defending Mr. Prlic, you would have put him on the stand with fewer witnesses, and I must go back to our original and continuous discussion concerning the procedure. This is an adversarial party-driven procedure with some aspects of civil law tradition. This is not a civil law tradition. There lies the problem. We have a case. We try to put on the case. We try to manage our time the best we could, given that we felt we had a lot of documents that we needed to put forward, because we needed to put on a defence, we needed to put on these documents, because you again, in your collective wisdom, decided not to allow us to put our documents during the Prosecution phase of the case. And there are motions and there are motions and there are motions on that, and the decisions continually come back and say, You can do that on your defence. So in light of all of that, to now make a suggestion, in open court, on the record, that Mr. Prlic entertain the notion of being a witness, while at the same time he's sitting here as an accused, given the fact that the Prosecution at that point, and I do believe they would be entitled to say as long as he -- once he takes the oath, they should be entitled to ask anything and everything under the sun, because they have an obligation. And so at this stage of the game, to be making these sorts of suggestions, Mr. President, I must say with all due frankness and respect, that I don't think this is a matter that can be taken lightly, it's not a matter that should be discussed in this format.
