utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things. First of all, you address the question of time again. As you know, the Trial Chamber granted you 95 hours, almost twice as much as the accused. When these 95 hours were given to you, a huge amount of work was done by the Trial Chamber, because on the basis of your witnesses and on the basis of the fact that Mr. Prlic was likely to testify, we had to decide how much time needed to be granted to you in an ideal world, so we spent a lot of time on this and the Trial Chamber decided that you would have 95 hours. And, believe me, when these 95 hours were given to you, the four Judges on this Bench, we were convinced that Mr. Prlic would testify, and to our surprise we looked at the witness list and Mr. Prlic's name was not on that list. Then this report, famous report, came in, and you know that for procedural reasons we were unable to admit it into evidence. This was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. But as a Judge, I feel that there is an important document that has been drafted by an accused in support of his defence, and this document is not part of the proceedings. What instruments do we have which would enable us to introduce this document, given that your time to put your case is over? So we have only one procedural possibility, and that is for your client to be called as a witness of the Court. He is entitled to refuse, of course. He can disagree. He can consult his lawyer. That's the only question I was putting to him. So you stand up and, as usual, make such blanket statements, and all we are trying to do is trying to find a solution for a thorny issue. Because of this problem, for a number of days Mr. Prlic was absent, which I believe is a prejudice for him, which prejudices him, and once again I'm trying to find a solution as regards this report. Of course, we can do without this report, if that is what you wish. It's whichever way you would like it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all -- with the most respect, the last comment that was made, I must say, was uncalled for. We have made every particular effort to get it in. We have tried to be as innovative as we possibly could, given the Rules. And I must say a great deal of improvisation is going on in this courtroom as well as other courtrooms because of time constraints. Now, when we were allotted a certain amount of time, we had to make certain decisions. And so, you were not present in the field when we met these witnesses, you were not present when we saw the mountains of documents presented to us, you were not there when we were out investigating. We had to put a case based on the allotted amount of time given to us. We didn't come up with just a number out of the blue. We studied the situation rather carefully. The number that we gave was rather precise. It was precise, based on experience, experience as trial lawyers; not as academicians, not as theoreticians, not as diplomats, not as judges, not as lay people, but as defence lawyers having gone through this process recognising that it takes a certain amount of time to get some things done. Now, when the Trial Chamber made its decision, you will note we did not appeal that decision, because we knew that that is a discretionary issue based, you know, on the Trial Chamber's observations, and so we recognised that even to have appealed, as others did, the Appeals Chamber was not going to do anything. So given that amount of time, we had to make some very painful choices, and we made them. And this is an adversarial process, I keep trying to inform the Trial Chamber, and once we make certain strategic, tactical, and operational decisions, at this point it's very difficult to then try to undo certain things. Now, if, by any chance, we were to entertain that, certainly I would be asking for an additional amount of time to get all these other documents in. We would be opening up certain other possibilities that we think we were not given at the time, as far as putting on our entire case. I should also say that as Mr. Prlic sits here, he is not some witness that the Trial Chamber can just call. He is an accused, and he has some certain fundamental rights. Now, I want that report in, he wanted it in. We tried to present the report as an extension of his oral statement, given that we did not have a sufficient amount of time. Frankly, I must say that I think the Trial Chamber, with all due respect, was absolutely wrong. The fact that the Appeals Chamber came back and said that you had the right to exercise your discretion, I think -- I see nothing wrong -- there's no contradiction there. I think the Trial Chamber could have very easily have said, Fine, exercising our discretion, we allow it, we'll give it whatever weight. For whatever reason, the Trial Chamber made that decision. All right. Now, I understand you want to try to get certain things in from the report. We would like to do the same thing. But this sort of issue cannot simply be brought up while Mr. Praljak takes leave and then put us in a position where I'm having to sit here to defend Mr. Prlic, and then to add insult to injury and say, Well, if you don't want the report in, then so be it. I just don't think that it is fair to the Prlic Defence. And I understand that there may be some aggravation on the part of members of the Bench that certainly do not like my approach to advocacy, but I can assure you that everything that we do, we do with deliberation. We may not do it perfectly, but we do it with deliberation. And I'm trying to be as respectful as I possibly can, while I'm trying to convey that we may have a cultural clash, cultural in the sense of two different legal cultures, the adversarial versus the civil law system. And I appreciate the Trial Chamber extending this invitation. I will certainly have a lengthy discussion with Mr. Prlic. But it's not a matter of me trying to hide something, or me not wanting something in, but I think the manner in which this was posed, out of the blue, does cause me a considerable amount of anxiety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can discuss this at length with Mr. Prlic, and you will let us know what your position is. This was just something I did on a personal note. And then we will see, afterwards, what it's to be. Let's proceed with Mr. Praljak, who has returned. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I continue with Mr. Praljak, I would like to express, recognising that this has just been raised as an initial possibility, grave concern on the part of the Prosecution, as a party to the case, to the extent that there may be some indication that the Trial Chamber is considering, if I can put it in a way, bending the Rules by calling an accused or facilitating a procedure whereby an accused can essentially augment his case as a vehicle to get additional exhibits tendered into evidence which, for whatever reason, right or wrong, were not successfully admitted into evidence during that accused's own case. It seems to me a very slippery slope, Mr. President, and I'm sure that the Prlic team is not the only party in this case that wishes it had more time and more opportunities to put on more evidence and to get more documents into evidence that were rejected during its own case. And so clearly the Prosecution would have views on such a procedure, if the Trial Chamber were wanting to consider that. And, again, that's just for the record at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Also for the record and in an effort, perhaps, to calm things down a bit further, I want to say that this was a very spontaneous reaction of the Chamber President. It has not been discussed among Judges at all at any moment, and it is, therefore, rather daring to attribute it to the Chamber, as such. I'm not -- I'm not -- I do not want now to take any personal position on this. We're not in the habit of discussing matters in the courtroom and in public. But I just want to make it clear that it's perhaps premature to panic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge is perfectly right. The other Judges have nothing to do with this question I put to Mr. Prlic, but any Judge is entitled to put questions. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we were talking about this testimony of Josip Praljak and about Mr. Tuta -- Mr. Naletilic having an office and a position in close proximity to Bruno Stojic. And for the time-frame, I can inform you, and this is from page 14801 of the transcript, that this testimony about -- from Josip Praljak relates to Exhibit 6170 -- P06170, which I think now, General, you have the document in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this document, this is a report of Josip Praljak, deputy warden of the Central Military Prison. It's dated the 27th of October, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Stringer. That's what the paper says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so this is a report on the work of the Detainee Release Commission, and it's a report that's drafted during the period of time that you are commander of the HVO Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But without the implications of the Main Staff having to do anything with this report. You can say, During the time while you commanded the Main Staff, two sheep dropped dead, and now you should be held responsible. Well, I've read the document, and to tell you the truth, I have no knowledge about it. I don't know anything about the event, and I did not receive such documents. Mr. Stringer, I can't or won't tell you anything about this document. That would be just speculating. You're telling me that I was somewhere at some time, and, for example, you asked me about the level of the Neretva River at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just continue with a few more questions, because I know that sometimes it seems rather a formality, but I do need to make a record on this. And for the record, can you agree with me that the date of this report, 27 October 1993, is a date during which you were in the position of commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Clearly, the extent to which the Judges wish to draw any connections between you and this document is left to them. The last question on this document is at the very bottom of the document or at the end of the document, and what we see here is that Josip Praljak is addressing this report both to Mladen Naletilic, aka Tuta, and also Mr. Bruno Stojic. So do I understand correctly from your testimony that you had no knowledge about any role Mr. Naletilic was playing in respect of the Detainee Release Commission that's referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, in the binder, the next exhibit is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a document before us. The Prosecutor draws a conclusion thereof. Mr. Praljak, on looking at this document, if you look at the first sentence, we understand why this report was drafted. Seemingly, Mr. Stojic gave an order on the 6th of August and referenced number 963/93, where clearly a commission is being established. This report relates to this commission. Now, whether -- the fact that Mr. Naletilic is an addressee of this report would confirm the idea that he was an advisor to Mr. Stojic. According to you, as the document states, can this have to do with the work conducted by the commission, without you having taken any part in this and without having any knowledge of it, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, Your Honours, these small problems you sometimes have with me occur precisely because I want to provide you with an answer that would give you as much of the factual truth as possible. Hence, I have no knowledge about this. I never did. I'm simply looking at a document that anyone can read, and I can't tell you anything about it that would not be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit in the binder should be P03910, 3910. Just take a moment, General. This exhibit actually consists of several different handwritten letters or fax messages, so why don't you take a moment to look those over and then I'll ask you a few questions about them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, General, these all appear to be from early August of 1993; at least the first two do. The first of these is a fax, and it's a handwritten message from Tuta to Minister Stojic, and what he's doing is making an assessment or a recommendation that a particular individual is suitable for the post of commander in Ljubuski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Recognising that you're --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. It says on the top the 3rd of August, but that doesn't necessarily need to make you conclude that this was sent on the 3rd of August. There is no date of reception, and sometimes the sending and receiving of documents was at odds, as you can see on the very next document. It was drafted on the 21st of July and received on the 3rd of August. Obviously, someone was stamping it upon receiving in the way they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's a good point, General, and you've noted it for us. I think my interest in this is a little more general than the specific dates, although obviously I agree that this straddles the period of time prior to and after which you became commander of the HVO Main Staff. To the extent that Mladen Naletilic was sending messages to Bruno Stojic on recommendations for those fit to command, were you aware at any time that Mladen Naletilic played such a role for the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that that was his role. This does resemble Tuta's signature, but still I don't know whether it is authentic, whether this document was sent at all. Mr. Stringer, there is nothing I can tell you that would be of any relevance about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I recognise -- and sometimes I ask you questions, I'm interested to know -- it's interesting for me even if you don't know. Okay, so I know that there are a lot of things that you do know, but I'm interested sometimes if you don't know. And my question simply here is: Did you know, as is indicated here, if Mladen Naletilic recommended persons for command positions to Bruno Stojic? If you didn't know that, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next one of these messages appears to have been received or stamped in the Main Staff -- or, I'm sorry, in the Defence Department on the same day, the 3rd of August. And as you've pointed out, it was sent on the 21st of July to Zagreb. And this appears to be a handwritten message to Gojko Susak from Tuta, and what he's doing here is asking that a couple of individuals, Mr. Mandic and Mr. Budimir, be allowed to join him. This raises an issue that's already been raised today by the President, which relates to the relationship between Mladen Naletilic and Gojko Susak. General, I think it's not in dispute that the three of you, yourself, Gojko Susak, and Mladen Naletilic, all knew each other or knew of each other as children back in Siroki Brijeg, when you were quite young.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I know that you -- I think it was yesterday you said that Mr. Tuta -- Mr. Naletilic was a couple of years younger and you didn't really go to school with him, but you knew each other.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Siroki Brijeg when I was 15 and a half. At that time, Mladen Naletilic could have been 12 or 12 and a half. Between that time and 1992, I did not see Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, so it was probably between 1960 and 1990. Let us not attach any attention to it that would only seem relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're aware that Mr. Susak and Mr. Tuta had similar experience, in that both of them left from the former Yugoslavia, they went abroad and lived outside of Yugoslavia, for many years, isn't that true, returning at the time that Yugoslavia began to fall apart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A similar path in that respect, yes. I know that Mr. Susak was also an emigre. I don't know which year, though. I know that Naletilic, Tuta, also left Yugoslavia at some point and lived abroad. In that regard, their life paths were similar, but not in any other aspect; I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, here we see in this message that Mr. Naletilic is sending a handwritten fax message. He addresses the minister of defence as "Gojko," so they appear to be on a first-name basis. Do you know whether they were good friends or whether they became good friends by virtue of their childhood background and other similar life experiences?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer. I personally think that they were not friends. It's one thing to have similar childhoods, which can serve as a precondition for a friendship, but Mr. Susak lived in Canada, Mr. Naletilic lived in Europe. What sort of connection they might have had, I don't know. This is a time span of about 20 years. In my view, one cannot call that a friendship.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mladen Naletilic had meetings with Gojko Susak in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say either "yes" or "no" to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, I'll put this to you: The fact that he can send handwritten fax messages to Gojko would indicate that Mr. Naletilic has some degree of influence with the Croatian Ministry of Defence. Would you agree with me that Mr. Tuta -- Mr. Naletilic did, in fact, have a level of influence with the Croatian Ministry of Defence during this period of time, July/August 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never had any information that would confirm your thesis that he had any sort of influence within the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. As for anyone writing texts such as this one in handwriting, well, that says more about that person trying to impose a certain type of communication. It says more about that person than about the document itself, or Mr. Susak, or the Ministry of Defence in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, recognising that -- well, if I understand correctly, General, you resigned from your position as assistant minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia at or about the time that you took command of the HVO Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So can you tell us whether on the 21st of July, 1993, were you still holding the position of assistant minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. However, by virtue of the fact that you had held that position for a number of months prior to July 21st of 1993, I have one question to ask you about the handling of this document. General, it appears that the document was faxed from Naletilic to Mr. Susak at the Croatian Ministry of Defence, as you pointed out, on or about the 21st of July, 1993, and we have at the same time a stamp of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna from the 3rd of August, 1993. So the question would be, General, whether you're aware of a procedure whereby documentation coming in to the Croatian Defence Ministry like this would have then been forwarded to the Defence Department of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that is completely impossible. I simply won't discuss whether the document is correct or not, whether it was planted or falsified. This should have a receipt stamp of the Ministry of Defence of Croatia. This is obviously in Singen, which is close to the Boden Lake where I worked, it's a German hotel or something of that sort. Obviously, Naletilic brought this with him. This shows the style. If the contents are correct, still I have to tell you that I can't testify to any aspect of this document. I can't tell you whether it was received in Croatia, whether it was sent, whether it came from Tuta, whether it was falsified. There's nothing I can tell you about it. You're trying to build on my ignorance. Methodologically speaking, it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: These two gentlemen, Captain Budimir and Lieutenant Ivica Mandic, do you know whether they ever came down to join Naletilic in action, as he's requesting here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply did not have that information. I have no idea that Mate Budimir and Ivica Mandic were down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know either of those gentlemen or did you know them at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many -- too many names that I had to keep in my head at the time. Therefore, I no longer remember the name. Perhaps if you showed me a photograph, I could tell you that I know them or I don't. But simply based on this, I can't say that I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to take the next document in the binder. I'm going to skip over one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you did not answer Mr. Stringer's question. It was a technical question. He sees these documents. These documents are faxed to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Susak. You will note that both documents are recorded on August 3rd in the Department of Defence, number 942/93, but a question springs to mind. These documents are recorded at the Department of Defence, but the document addressed to Mr. Susak, could you tell us whether this document is directly going to be faxed to Zagreb, through the DOD? That was the question that was asked to you, and you did not answer it. Maybe you don't know, but then please say so. Or you might have ideas as to what has happened, and then tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you said that it was sent through? I'm afraid I didn't understand. By what means? I didn't understand the technical aspect of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me come back -- go back on this. Mr. Naletilic is sending two documents, handwritten documents. We both have these two documents at hand. These two documents arrive at the Department of Defence on August 3rd. There's a recording number, there's a log number. The first one is for Mr. Stojic. Whether Mr. Stojic read it or not, that's another problem. But the second one is for Mr. Susak. Could you tell us what's going to happen to this? Is it going to go into the waste basket because Mr. Susak has nothing to do with the DOD, or is it going to be forwarded by fax to Zagreb? I believe that this is what Mr. Stringer wanted to know, and the Judges also would like to know what could have happened to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, if you sent this to Zagreb, then that must have been received and archived in Zagreb, or maybe Gojko Susak simply threw it away. But if this was an official document received by the Ministry of Defence, it should have been archived. That's one thing. Another thing. My question is: If the assumption is correct that Tuta was next-door to Bruno Stojic, why would he have to write to him? He would just go through the door and say, Listen, Mr. Stojic, I want this and that. I'm simply thinking logically. I know that in the Ministry of Defence, once a document was received by fax, it needs to be archived. Whether this was archived or stamped 9 or 12 days later, that's completely unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if you would please turn to the next document in the binder. It's P01572, and this is the telephone directory of the Mostar HVO Main Staff. That's what's indicated on the front page. And then there are entries for various persons and phone number extensions within the Defence Department of the HZ-HB. And this one relates to March of 1993, so recognising that it's not the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, although it is a time that relates to our case. If you look within the Defence Department, you'll see that it has Mr. Stojic as the head, and then it has his deputy, Slobodan Bozic. This is -- the ERN number for the page, the relevant page, General, ends with the number 4306. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So here on this -- on this telephone list, underneath the deputy of the Defence Department, we see an entry for "ATG-Tuta," and then it has the name "Mladen Naletilic" there and it's got his telephone extension number. So, again, this relates to a couple of questions I've asked you in the past. First of all, this "ATG-Tuta," that's referred to, do you know whether that would indicate that the "ATG-Tuta" would fall within this group of units that were classified as professional or special-purpose units on the chart I was showing you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that would automatically follow. I can't say. It reads "ATG-Tuta," "Mladen Naletilic," March 1993. How would one arrive at that? Why would that automatically mean that? Why, then, do other units not have their phone numbers right there? No, I don't think so. I think the logic is a bit twisted if we conclude, by default, that that is what it means. I can't give you any reliable information on this. As far as the logic of this is concerned, I think you can deal with the Judges, as far as that is concerned. My logic is not the same as yours. Mine, for instance, is not the same. I'm trying to look into the facts. You're asking me about the facts. You can give us your theories, and then it will eventually be down to the Chamber to tell us what they think about your logic and whether the weight of the documents is more on the side of my guilt or on the side of my innocence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you'll turn the page, for section number 4, there's a section there for the Main Staff, HVO Mostar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, of course, being from March of 1993, this would have Milivoj Petkovic as the commander, and then it continues down.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief, chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Chief. And if you turn the page, we see other units, such as Bruno Busic, for example, which is one of the ones we were talking about yesterday. So, General, the question is whether, and I think you've already given the answer, whether this document, in your opinion, is one that we can rely on or look to if we're looking to classify the various units of the HVO armed forces, and whether they would have been more closely linked to the Main Staff or to the Defence Department. I think your answer is, no, that we cannot make any conclusions based on this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I have an objection. If one looks closely at this directory, you will see, under number 4, the Main Staff, and then there is an independent, number 5, individual military units, the Bruno Busic Regiment and onwards. I don't think it is fair to see these two, number 4 and number 5, as one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we agree on that, Mr. President. I think that was the reason for my last question to the general, where I suggested that you cannot use this document as a way to classify the various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, sir. Based on this, one can draw no inference other than that there were phones. I told you everything I knew about the Bruno Busic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware -- would you have been aware that in March of 1993, Mr. Naletilic appeared in that location on this phone list, with his own telephone extension within the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in no way aware of that at the time. I came and I went, I did some work there. You know the periods of time involved. It is only logical that I would not have gone into anything like that, and I wasn't interested. I was entirely involved in something altogether different. I had no knowledge of that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next Exhibit is P09533. And, General, you'll see this is also a telephone directory. It's for a later period of time, which appears to be the 27th of September, 1993, as the date -- as a date that's written on the document. And, of course, this relates now to the period of time that you're commander of the Main Staff. And here, again, we see "Tuta," on this telephone directory, again, within the Defence Department, according to this. So the question, then, is: During this period of time, October 1993 -- excuse me, September 1993, when you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, were you aware that Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, maintained a telephone extension and his name appeared on the telephone list within the HVO Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have no information indicating anything like that, about how the numbers were copied. But what I find noteworthy is there is no fax number next to Tuta's name, so which fax was it that he used to fax his documents? I don't know. But then, again, I do have to say I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, General, is P090 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a small detail here in this document. We have material evidence here. Mr. Praljak, we know that offices always have extensions. You know, if you visit the office of the Judges, will you see that there is a number -- an office number, office number. There's an office number for Mr. Tuta. Obviously, his office number is 24, which means that physically, materially, he did have an office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. I do apologise for this intervention. It reads here "local number," local number at the switchboard. That is not the office number, what you read as 24. It's the specific number of the specific office, it's the number that is used at the switchboard to reach a particular office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In your own language, Mr. Praljak, what does "lokal" mean? Is it "extension"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means you call the switchboard and you ask for this internal number, or you dial it yourself. There's a beep, normally, or you speak to the operator, and then you ask to be put through to this internal number. That's what it means, "lokal," internal number. This goes through the switchboard. A lot of numbers go through the switchboard, and the switchboard couldn't handle all these numbers were it not for these internal numbers. That's what it means, or in-house numbers, if you like. I can provide more detail, if you like. But, Mr. Stringer, if you look at this: "HVO Mostar Main Staff commander," you see what it says there. I was never based -- my command was never based in Mostar, but rather in Citluk. This was probably copied or Xeroxed just like that. This is not true. It reads "27th of September, HVO Mostar Main Staff commander." The commander and the Main Staff were, in fact, in Citluk, not in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General, but getting -- I apologise, Mr. President. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So getting back to the main point for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just coming back on this last question, there is, in the first column, something which I would suppose is something like the area code, and we see that there are two different area codes used. One is "058," and the other is "088." I just wonder, pure technically, whether Tuta having 058, but it's the same as the president, but probably not -- could not be a different location, could it? This must be a Mostar office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. 058, if you remember, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, was a prefix for the Split switchboard, and then you would call them, they would put you through to Zagreb, and you could speak to the entire world. 088 was the local switchboard, the old one. Those who didn't have 058, the call sign, could only make local calls, but you needed to get through to 058 in order to reach anyone outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, be it Vitez or Sarajevo you were calling from. If you wanted to call someone from the outside world, as it were, you needed to go through that. After 1992, the switchboard in Mostar was destroyed and the coaxial cable was hit, and then the switchboard, and then the directional linked to Sarajevo, and so on and so forth. But there were few of these numbers because it was a small switchboard, and one used the 058 as a call sign and then you had 02032, and you could use small local offices to use those small devices to switch on to the operator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It then follows that this prefix gives no indication as to where the ultimate telephone apparel is located. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But it does indicate, General, that if someone has the 058 area code, then that person has a greater ability or a greater range of places he or she can contact; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as America or even further afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'm not fully convinced, Mr. Praljak. Let's assume that someone calls Mr. Tuta. In order to call him, he will dial 526-574, I assume, with the Mostar area code before that. This then reaches the Defence Department. The switchboard operator will then, on his keyboard, transfer the call on number 24. You are a telephone expert. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 058 is a direct link to -- if you go through that, you can choose anything that is switched on to that switchboard and goes to Split. If you call 088, you go to the switchboard first, and then they put you through, regardless of whether you're inside the building or outside the building. It depends on how the switchboard is structured. They put you through because you use a smaller number of telephone lines. For example, Your Honours, if we have no lines for all the Judges and all the persons in this courtroom to actually have a connection, we'll try to get one line up, or three, and then we'll branch from these to individual connections for everyone: Judge Trechsel, number 2; Judge Antonetti, number 1. You will get these numbers. And then this man calls and he says, I want to speak to Judge Trechsel, and then he switches over to number 2. There is a socket there, you remember the old type of socket that we used, or there is automatic dialing, there is a sound signal. And then you dial to "2," and then this switchboard, the internal switchboard, directs this to a particular individual, because the outgoing connections were too few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My fellow Judge tells me that it is time to have a break, and it is 20 past 12.00. We will take this opportunity to place some phone calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer. Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Your Honour's leave, and Mr. Stringer's, of course, during the break there were two things that occurred to me, if I may be allowed to present them. First of all, I'm looking at these pages that were faxed. There is nothing on them indicating that they were faxed. Each time you send something through a fax machine, what you get on that page is two things; the date the fax was sent and the phone number from which it was sent. There is also the number of pages that eventually got through. Unfortunately, I don't see these marks on any of these pages that allegedly Mr. Naletilic faxed. That is the first thing I wish to say. The second thing is this: I'm looking at this fax that he allegedly sent to Gojko Susak. It reads: "Dunja, send the document through to my fax number, 700-128." And then what I did, this -- the first three digits, 700, indicate a place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "700" stands for Siroki Brijeg. If you look at the directory, you can clearly see that that is the case. It reads: "Siroki Brijeg, commander of the Signal Centre, MUP Military Police," 701, 704, starting with 088, 700, all the numbers are like that. It is with a high degree of suspicion that I can state that this wasn't, in fact, faxed, because it bears no standard fax marks. Secondly, Mr. Naletilic refers to a phone number here, and the phone number is obviously in Siroki Brijeg for this to be faxed back to him, if anything at all. These were the two technical matters that I wished to raise, and I can elaborate if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, the general was talking about P03910, which we discussed earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just staying with this exhibit for a moment, now that you've brought us back to it, can you and I agree that they appear to have been received within the Defence Department of the HVO on or about the 3rd of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp is there. Nevertheless, based on all of the aforementioned, I have a well-founded suspicion, Mr. Stringer. It is quite clear here that he refers to a fax number in Siroki Brijeg. How that reached the Defence Department, I simply don't know. It wasn't by fax. Did someone perhaps bring the pages over, physically? I don't know, but my suspicion is great. If this had been faxed anywhere else, the fax number would have been clearly legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P0 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. If I may help, probably, because the stamp is not really readable completely, but it looks like it is the stamp -- on the top of the document, it is the stamp in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whatever institution that might be. It is not stamped of an institution in Zagreb. Even though it is not very clear, but it looks like the words are here "Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, that's correct, I agree. I think this is the stamp of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. I just thought that maybe it would help to clear up that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I asked my question, remember that I had talked about the Defence Department, so it is clear that the stamp can only be that of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P09043 in your binder. General, I think --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you don't have flu, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I smoke too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reassured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I smoke like a chimney.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you should stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, I should, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this is a photograph. It was shown to you, actually, when you testified in the Tuta Stela trial back in April of 2002. Do you recognise this photo? Do you remember seeing this before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is this a photo that was taken at the time of the funeral of Mario Hrkac, whose nickname was Cikota, that occurred in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. It's been a long time, though. I can't be positive about it, but it's highly probable. I had to go to dozens, evens hundreds of funerals. In our culture, it's just something that you must do. When you knew a person and that person died, or their family, you had to go to that funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Mario Hrkac was a commander of HVO soldiers who was killed during the operation at Sovici/Doljani in mid-April of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, sir. I had heard that he was killed. I knew him from back in 1992, the operation near Mostar. I probably went for that reason. This was a time when I was in Mostar. I went over to the eastern side, so I attended the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this funeral, where did it take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Siroki Brijeg cemetery, I think, the Catholic cemetery at Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after this funeral and in the weeks that followed, is it correct that an HVO unit was named or perhaps renamed as the Mario Hrkac, Cikota, brigade or unit in honour of this person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. That might be the case, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this picture we see an elderly couple standing in the front, and then behind them we see some men standing in camouflage uniforms. And can we agree, General, that you're the person who, on this photo, appears in the far left corner?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, far left corner, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then standing next to you, the man also in camouflage who is balding, who is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vice Vukojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Vukojevic a member of the -- well, you tell me, General, did he hold a position in the Croatian government at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Vukojevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We go back to way before the war. He spent a lot of time in prison. He was an individual who was marked out as a nationalist. Those were the charges against him. In the former Yugoslavia, I think he spent a total of six to seven years in prison for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, he's with you, standing, in a uniform. Did he hold a position in the HVO at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did he hold a position in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. I think for a while he held a post in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, but I don't know which post exactly or, indeed, at what time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then next to him there's a gentleman in camouflage uniform, wearing glasses. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Andabak, one of the Andabaks mentioned. Ivan Andabak, that's his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And his position was that of deputy commander of the Convicts Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he called me to check the plan for the liberation of Orlovac, and that operation, in 1992, he was the commander. That was my information. At the time, there was fighting with the JNA in Capljina. He was involved in some talks with UNPROFOR. He was quite fluent in Spanish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me repeat my question. At the time of this funeral, Ivan Andabak held the position of deputy commander of the Convicts Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. As I said, at the time I talked to him in 1992, he was a commander. He was the commander of the Convicts Battalion, or at least that's how he was introduced to me at the time. I don't know what post he held at this particular point in time depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then standing next to him, as we continue to move to the right across this photograph, there's another man a bit shorter with glasses. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was -- well, I was going to ask you what his position was at this time, and I think you've already given us your evidence on that, that you don't know what his position or his function was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it true that soldiers under his command were active in the operation in Sovici/Doljani that occurred on or about the 16th/17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, nor did I at the time. Anything else would constitute speculation on my part. My answer simply has to be: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. The next exhibit, General, is P02902. And I should say that this document, being a report of the Spanish Battalion, is confidential, so that I believe we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, your previous answer was somewhat surprising. The Prosecutor asked you whether you knew anything about Sovici/Doljani. You say, No. Fair enough. You go to the funeral. Like all of us, we've all attended funerals. When you attend a funeral, generally you ask what the person died of, normally speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't say -- well, first of all, I did not hold a post at the time, at the time of this funeral in April. That was when I switched over to the left bank. I explained about that. These weren't my soldiers, nor did I, in fact, hold any sort of position, nor, indeed, was I aware of what was going on in Sovici or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. But you attend this funeral, and on this photograph we see Mr. Naletilic, Andabak, and other people, so you are all mourning the person. And, generally, after the funeral, you shake hands with the bereaved and then people discuss matters. And you didn't think of turning to Naletilic and Andabak and asking how he had died. Perhaps he died in -- whether he died in action or not; you didn't discuss this at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir, not at the funeral. I did hear that he had been hit by a sniper on a hill, and then I went away. The funeral was not the place to discuss that, especially because I was there only for a short time. I did know that guy. In 1992, he participated in the liberation of Orlovac. And then we moved on to liberate the whole of the right bank of the Neretva, for which purpose I used all of the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, P02902 is a report of the Spanish Battalion. We can talk about it in court, but it's confidential and so it can't be shown outside the courtroom on the monitors. General, this one is dated the 23rd of June, 1993, and I want to take you to -- actually, it's -- the actual report that we're going to look at is dated the 22nd of June, 1993. I'm looking at page 3 of the English version. Under paragraph 1, "Area of Responsibility," if you continue to move down you'll see paragraph 1.2 is for areas, and the first area there is Mostar. And if you continue down through the document, the next area that's mentioned is Jablanica/Konjic. That's the part where I want to ask my first question. What this says is: "Jablanica has continued to be shelled throughout the day, shelling being more intense between 9.00 and 11.00." Do you see that, General? Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "The main targets are the Unis factory, hydroelectric power-station, [indiscernible] hotel, Policija Headquarters, and the hydro-electrical power-station offices." And then it gives an indication of where the shelling is coming from. And then it says: "Other information: 1. Fierce fighting in the area of Boksevica is continuing. HVO troops are under the command of General Praljak and Colonel Miro Andric. In the area, there are HVO troops of Jusuf Prazina, Juka, and Mladen Naletilic, aka Tuta." Now, General, I know you've told us that you don't know what Tuta's function was during this period of time. Is it true that he was, in fact, fighting with HVO units with you in the Boksevica area in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. When I arrived at Boksevica as a volunteer, an individual, I later received approval from Mr. Stojic [as interpreted], but Boksevica had been completed by that time. The operation was supposed to include the regaining of territory on that mountain which had been lost for the HVO so as to be able to extract civilians. Mr. Miro Andric, the colonel, was not at Boksevica, that is not correct, and Jusuf Prazina and Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, were not with me either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I have a correction to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's not the HV, but the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 80, line 1, it says that General Praljak received approval of Mr. Stojic, whereas the witness actually said "Mr. Petkovic." This is to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, is that correct, that you said "Petkovic" and not "Stojic"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, I said "Petkovic," and not "Stojic." And you said "HV units," but it should be "HVO units."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if I said "HV," I meant to say, "HVO," so that's my mistake. And I don't think you need to elaborate further, General. So what you're saying is that you dispute this document to the extent that it says that Tuta was fighting in the area of Boksevica at the time you were there in June of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. While I was there, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was not there, and Miro Andric wasn't there, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you about in this document is actually in the preceding section. Just above "Jablanica-Konjic," there's a comment, and it says: "There is a continuous accumulation of HVO weapons and material in the city, reaching levels that lead us to think that there may be major operations in the not-too-distant future." General, recognising that you were not in Mostar, itself, but that you were in the vicinity of Mostar, in the Boksevica area, were you aware, sir, that - this is prior to the 30th of June, 1993 - the HVO continued to amass weapons in Mostar in potentially a preparation for major military operations against the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Stringer, Mount Boksevica, where I spent many days, was completely cut off. No information could reach the top of the hill, where there were only two shacks and corpses of animals rotting away. No information could come in, except for the one when we decided, together with the commanders, to pull the soldiers and inhabitants out. That was the only purpose of it. Secondly, the HVO had no weapons to amass anywhere. Everything the HVO had had already been deployed, and we were always short of it. Whenever we received anything, it would be sent to the lines immediately. These were wrong conclusions of someone from a different army which was structured and supplied differently. This has nothing to do with the HVO whatsoever. How could we amass weapons when we hardly had any weapons of any quality?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Continuing to move upward, I've got a question about some of the text that is in the section on Mostar. And under the Mostar section, it says, in paragraph 1, that: "At 22 1000 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. I am very sorry to interrupt you. I only would like to ask a follow-up question here concerning the very last sentence of the answer given by Mr. Praljak. He said, and I will quote, in his answer: "How could we amass weapons when we hardly had any weapons of any quality?" Now, I somehow -- I feel that I'm at a loss when I heard this, and I re-read it again, this sentence because as we know, we have heard from a number of witnesses here who have already told us and who have witnessed to the transfer of weapons to the BiH Army, so that is why I see a certain contradiction in itself, if Mr. Praljak now says that, How could we amass weapons when we hardly had any weapons of any quality. And I hope that he will clarify this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, when you compare what a regular corps of any professional army has, this is what I had in mind. And when you compare that to what an HVO corps had, the HVO was below any level. When -- in a corps you have seven or eight tanks, individually speaking, these are quality pieces, but seven or eight tanks deployed along a 100-kilometre line is insignificant. It cannot amount to amassing weapons. One could amass weapons if you had 100 tanks in supply and you transfer 50 of them to the lines. But if you have 10, 12, or 15 guns covering that area which had already been deployed, then we cannot talk about any amassing of weapons. "Amassing" means bringing in, in the military sense, bringing in of new forces and new tanks from another area. We didn't have any of that. We were stretched out. And the same, of course, applied to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some weapons did come in, but if you compare that to the staffing and amounts of weaponry possessed by an American or a French brigade, that is incomparable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this report talks about an incident that occurred on the 22nd of June at 10.00 in the morning, which I believe that's correct, with the format that they use in here. It says: "At 22 1000, when the incoming company was making its way to the detachment to proceed with the relief operation, the last three armoured half-tracks were detained at the check-point at the southern entrance on the main road. Personnel manning the check-point made an attempt to search the interior of the vehicles before allowing them through." And then the next paragraph talks about SpaBat officers who met with representatives of the HVO, including, it has here, Mr. Lukic, head of security for the HVO: "After talks, the company was allowed to proceed into Mostar." Secondly: "In a Croatian Television broadcast this afternoon, viewers were told that ammunition and mortars had been discovered inside the vehicles detained at the check-point on the access road to Mostar and that the weapons, in its opinion, were being transported by UNPROFOR to the Muslim Army. The truth of the matter is that these vehicles belonged to the company's Mostar section which was making its way to Mostar." And then skipping down to the last paragraph of this section, there's a comment that says: "How the Croat community will react vis-a-vis UNPROFOR after the propaganda broadcast over Croat TV cannot be predicted. There might well be a further worsening in relations which are already at a low ebb." Now, General, I want to take this incident, this report, to put to you that the HVO, first of all, controlled access to Mostar, despite what you say. It controlled access to Mostar both from the north and the south, and that if -- well, let me just put that to you. Isn't that true? Because you've indicated otherwise in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is the north mentioned anywhere in here? You say "from the north and the south." I was quite precise. As of the 30th of June, when the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina attacked the HVO, the army had an open way to the north throughout the conflict. This is what I can confirm. Therefore, we can only discuss the south. Secondly, not even the elementary facts of this report are correct. There is no "Akram" in the HVO. It was probably Mr. Akrap. Then there was no Lukic who was chief of security. It was probably Ivo Lucic. So even that personal information is incorrect. And they had discussions with those people for months preceding that. Thirdly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just finish this. I'm going to try to cut you off to stream-line this a bit. Are you telling us -- I recognise you're challenging the report. Are you telling us that you reject the Spanish Battalion's report here, which indicates that they were stopped at an HVO check-point and had to negotiate their way through? Can we at least agree that that is something that the SpaBat would at least know about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is highly likely that the information about them being stopped at a certain point towards the south is correct because they transported mortars which belonged to their mortar section, and the HVO believed, whether reasonably or not, that they intended to give or sell those mortars to the Army of B and H. There was such information to that effect. I don't know whether this one was, but most of it proved to be correct because we came across such weapons. It was because of that, probably, that they were stopped and everything followed from it. But I don't think anything of the sort could have happened towards the north, especially not after the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the fact is that after talking with these high-level -- fairly high-level people within the HVO, including the head of its Security Sector, Mr. Lucic, that the HVO used this incident to spin it into a propaganda incident that was then broadcast on Croat TV to create tensions and quite possibly to put UNPROFOR in a more dangerous situation vis-a-vis the Croat population there; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not an HVO television. Secondly, any television station is free to present information any way they see fit. Because of the fact that someone saw some information or heard some information on TV, that is not enough to bring you to any conclusions. The issue at hand is that they had mortars. Whether they intended to sell them or hand them over, I don't know. I know about some information from Croatia that millions of litres of oil were sold to the Serbs by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it's your position here that the mortars on these SpaBat vehicles were, in fact, going to be turned over to the ABiH forces on East Mostar? Is that the accusation you're making?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my wildest dreams. I only said that those who probably did this had their reasons to suspect, and they wanted to see whether any weapons were being transported to the enemy side. I would never assert anything of that sort without solid proof, but there may have been grounds for suspicion, and then that needs to be followed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in your answer a few moments ago, you said that: "First of all, it was not an HVO television." And I don't know if I misspoke, but I don't think I said that. The report here is that it's Croat television, not HVO television. But the fact is that the publication of this sort of propaganda, as it's classified here, would, indeed, put UNPROFOR forces in Mostar and the region in danger, if in fact the public thought that SpaBat was equipping the ABiH with artillery; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Why would that put a well-armed force in danger? And, secondly, that doesn't need to be propaganda, but a report broadcast, and dozens of TV stations had their broadcasts and sent information of their choosing which, for the most part, was in keeping with the policy of their respective countries and governments. And I have seen that in quantities beyond any tolerable measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unless there are more questions on this document, Mr. President, I'm ready to move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P04131, General, I believe is the next document in your binder, 4131. Do you recognise this, General? This is an order that you issued on the 12th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was signed by General Petkovic. I signed it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you accept this as an order that was issued by you or with your -- based on your authority as commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have no reason to change this order. I only think that the ATG-Tuta, whatever it was called, was shorthand for Baja Kraljevic, the unit commanded by Mr. Predrag Mandic. But if Mr. Petkovic comes to testify, you could ask that of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Stringer. I have a correction for the transcript. I have a correction, nothing more. Page 87, line 10, to your question the general said: "This is an order that was signed by General Petkovic." And I don't want to suggest any answers to the general, but I would kindly ask him to repeat what his relationship with the order is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is typed there. Since I was absent, General Petkovic must have signed it on my behalf. I agree with all of its contents, save for the "ATG-Tuta" reference which I believe was the unit called Baja Kraljevic, but in shorthand the other term was used. Mr. Petkovic is better equipped to explain this, should he find himself in this seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to go through this document in greater detail. It's an order related to the command structure in the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB. It's issued by you or with your approval somewhat early on, after you've taken command of the HVO Main Staff, and so my first question to you is why it was deemed necessary to issue such an order or whether this order constitutes some sort of a change in the hierarchy from that which existed previously.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you can see the orders on the implementation of disciplinary measures and the laws of war is something that kept reoccurring, and that was for the reason that the overall social and military system of Herceg-Bosna was on the verge of breaking up. One could hardly even call it a system. And here we have assumptions that this was some sort of an American system or something of that nature, whereas it wasn't. From the outset, we had to repeat same things all over again, because the system was caving in. The social pillars could no longer bear the weight of that war. Much as in cases of natural disasters, things kept caving in, and then you start building again and then it caved in again, so it was going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to let you speak so that you can give the fuller answer that you want, but you've got to try to be a little more selective in the number of words that you use. I'm trying to focus on this specific order. Correct me if I'm wrong. Is it correct, then, based on what you've just said, that the intent of this order was to try to reaffirm or reassert a particular chain of command within the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, who, by what means, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 1 here, it states that the Main Staff of the HZ-HB armed forces shall be directly subordinated to the supreme commander of the armed forces of the HZ-HB. Now, that supreme commander is Mate Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this just confirms, again, what you've said previously, that you had a direct -- it was Boban who was your direct superior and not, for example, Bruno Stojic, even though Stojic was the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then this continues in the next paragraph to say that the Main Staff exerts direct command over the operative zones, and it lists the operative zones there. Then it continues to identify professional units. Well, let's just go through this one by one. We've covered this some already in the testimony yesterday with the chart. This is consistent with what you said yesterday, that the Main Staff exerts direct command over the operative zones; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the next is professional units, Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic Regiments, and again you indicated to us yesterday that those were two professional units over which the Main Staff exerted direct command; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, speaking of the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The RTP, which I have as Rocket and Artillery Regiment, and also the Air Force Group, these are units that are directly subordinated to the Main Staff, then; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Air Force Group was the one that had helicopters and transported those wounded only. The ATG-Tuta, to repeat -- sorry, that was not the question? Sorry? Yes, I'm tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There's a conversation taking place here between the witness and his counsel, and I'm not a party to it, which makes me uncomfortable. General, before you jump ahead to the Tuta ATG, I'd like to stay for a minute with the Rocket and Artillery Regiment. Okay?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please, I'm just a little tired. Did you ask me about the other thing? That was the only issue. Please don't hold it against me. I do not mean any harm. This has gone on now for several hours, so I am getting a little worse for wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Perhaps, given the fact that the time is near -- Mr. Praljak seems a little tired. He claims we can press on, but it still might be a good idea to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, it's up to you. I've already said so. You know, answering questions over for hours and hours, especially when you're under stress because you're an accused, it's just something that is exhausting. If you're exhausted, tell us if you want to stop and we can just stop the proceedings. There's just 10 minutes left. It's up to you, really.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have the poor habit of not being able to eat in the morning, and then I smoke a number of cigarettes, and then sometimes some details of the questions escape me a little, slip my attention. I'm much better off, in that respect, in the afternoon because I'm more attentive. I think it might be a good idea to stop the proceedings, just to prevent any confusion from arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we stop, there is a technical request that I have. General Praljak was given another two binders yesterday with questions from the Prosecutor. Many of these documents are comprehensive documents; presidential transcripts, reports, SpaBat reports, and such-like, a lot of it in evidence already. I think we might be saving a lot of time if we allow General Praljak to take these binders with him. We had yesterday at least three situations where we couldn't agree on the correct pages or which transcript we were talking about, and it took a while to resolve. Most of these documents have been disclosed already; no surprises there. Nevertheless, it might be a good idea for the general to have a look so we can move along faster tomorrow. I see no reason for the Prosecutor to oppose this, especially given the fact that most of these documents have been exhibited already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all depends on Mr. Stringer. He's in charge of his cross-examination. It's up to him to decide. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the Trial Chamber knows and as all of the counsel know, throughout this long trial, the practice has been that the witnesses do not take the exhibits away with them on cross-examination. I don't think it's fair to put this witness, even though he's an accused, in a favoured position in respect of all of the other witnesses, both Prosecution and Defence, who've appeared and who've not been allowed to take documents away and study them in advance of being cross examined about them, and so the Prosecution position is we would oppose that. I don't think it would save much time. Actually, I think it's gone fairly smoothly with the current practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do accept that. I do take the Prosecutor's word that that was the norm. Sometimes General Praljak must be allowed sufficient time to study the documents and see what they're about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the binders will stay in the courtroom. They'll stay here, anyway. And we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of August, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Coric and Pusic not present]
